name: Silver
spiritual: Acts as a conductor of intention
physical: Traditionally associated with cool, calm energy
Kept nearby for comfort during stress
Folk traditions link silver jewelry to clearer feeling
summary: Native silver forms wiry, branching sprays and nuggets of bright metal, linked in tradition to the Moon, intuition, reflection and calm communication.
intro: Native silver is silver as nature made it: curling wires, fern-like sprays and dendritic crystals that look like silver hair and tarnish to grey and black. The best specimens come from Kongsberg in Norway, from Mexico and from Ontario. It is soft, around 2.5 to 3, and it is the best conductor of electricity of all metals. Fresh silver is bright white, but it darkens in air with a thin layer of silver sulfide. Crystal lovers treasure silver as the lunar metal, a reflective, intuitive presence that pairs naturally with moonstone, quartz and pearls.
history: Silver has been mined for more than 5,000 years, with early centers in Anatolia and the Greek mines at Laurion. It was a currency metal and a symbol of the Moon in alchemy, with the symbol of a crescent. The Spanish conquest of the Americas centered on the silver mines of Potosi in Bolivia and Zacatecas in Mexico, which transformed global trade. It was used in mirrors, coins, tableware and photography. Traditions across cultures link silver with purity and protection from harm. In crystal practice it is used as the setting and conductor for stones.
meaning: Crystal practitioners treat silver as the metal of the Moon, associated with reflection, intuition and emotional flow. It is linked to the third eye and throat, and used to support calm communication and honest self-reflection. Practitioners say silver amplifies the energy of stones set in it and brings a cool, lunar balance to fiery ones. Emotionally it is associated with calm and grace. Silver jewelry is a long-standing personal talisman for clarity and protection in folk tradition. Traditionally it is also linked to cool, balanced energy. Native silver specimens are cherished by collectors and are often displayed with moonstone.
howToUse: Wear silver jewelry set with stones to carry their energy, especially with moonstone, clear quartz or labradorite. Hold a native silver specimen during moonlit meditation and focus on a question. Place a piece on an altar for lunar rituals, new moon intentions and dream work. Use silver wire to wrap stones or link them in a grid. A specimen on a windowsill can catch moonlight, which many practitioners enjoy.
care: Silver tarnishes in air and sulfur, turning grey or black. Polish jewelry with a soft silver cloth and store in an airtight bag with an anti-tarnish strip. Raw specimens should be kept dry and handled by the matrix, because the wires are delicate and oils can darken them. Cleanse with sound, smoke, moonlight or brief sun. Avoid rubber, wool and harsh chemicals that speed tarnish.
identify: Native silver is soft, malleable and silver-white when fresh, with wire or dendritic forms, tarnishing to grey or black. It leaves a silver-white streak. It is often confused with acanthite, bismuth, platinum and silvery metals like tin or aluminum. A magnet will not attract it. Many shop specimens are actually cast or lab-grown, so ask about origin. Genuine silver jewelry is stamped 925 for sterling.

faq.q: Why is silver linked to the Moon?
faq.a: Since ancient times silver has been paired with the Moon in alchemy and astrology, thanks to its pale, reflective shine. Crystal practitioners use it for intuition, reflection and lunar rituals.
Silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air to form a dark layer of silver sulfide. Polishing with a soft cloth removes it, and storing silver in an airtight bag slows it down.

Specimens of native silver, especially in fine wire or dendritic forms, are uncommon and sought by collectors. Much of the silver you see sold as crystal specimens may be lab-grown or cast, so ask about the source.
